cards.statement: A producer can attach metadata headers to an individual Kafka record.
cards.explanation: Record headers carry application metadata alongside the key and value.

cards.statement: Kafka removes a retained record when a consumer reads it successfully.
cards.explanation: Reading a retained event leaves it available for later reads.
cards.misconception: Consumption deletes records.

cards.statement: Kafka spreads a topic's partitions over several brokers of the cluster.
cards.explanation: A topic's partitions are buckets placed on different brokers, so client applications can read and write one topic through many brokers at the same time.

cards.statement: Kafka assigns offsets from a shared sequence spanning a topic's partitions.
cards.explanation: Kafka tracks an independent offset sequence for each partition.
cards.misconception: Offsets are unique across a whole topic.

cards.statement: A broker with auto.create.topics.enable=true creates a missing topic when a KafkaConsumer subscribes.
cards.explanation: allow.auto.create.topics defaults to true on the consumer, so the broker's auto.create.topics.enable decides whether a subscribed missing topic is created.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: Kafka preserves publication order across the partitions of a topic.
cards.explanation: Kafka guarantees publication order within a partition.
cards.misconception: A topic has a single order spanning its partitions.

cards.statement: Adding partitions keeps the default producer's existing key-to-partition mapping intact.
cards.explanation: Increasing the partition count changes the default key mapping.
cards.misconception: Partition expansion preserves the existing key mapping.

cards.statement: Kafka lets an existing topic shrink its partition count in place.
cards.explanation: Kafka supports increasing an existing topic's partition count, rather than reducing it.
cards.misconception: An existing topic can shrink its partition count.

cards.statement: Kafka stores a record sent alone by a producer inside a record batch.
cards.explanation: Kafka always writes records in record batches; a batch holds one or more records, so a lone record is stored as a single-record batch.

cards.statement: Kafka brokers keep compressed record batches compressed in the log.
cards.explanation: The on-disk batch format stores the compressed record data.

cards.statement: Kafka judges a segment's time retention by its earliest record timestamp.
cards.explanation: The largest record timestamp determines a segment's retention age.
cards.misconception: The oldest record determines segment expiration.

cards.statement: retention.bytes caps the combined log size of a topic's partitions.
cards.explanation: Kafka applies retention.bytes separately to each partition.
cards.misconception: Size retention is a topic-wide storage cap.

cards.statement: Kafka leaves size-based log retention unlimited by default.
cards.explanation: Kafka enables a storage-size retention limit when configured.

cards.statement: segment.ms makes Kafka roll a segment even when segment.bytes has room.
cards.explanation: A time-based roll closes a segment before its size limit is reached.

cards.statement: Kafka uses log compaction for topic cleanup by default.
cards.explanation: The default cleanup.policy is delete, which expires old segments.
cards.misconception: Topics use compaction by default.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.2, an empty cleanup.policy keeps log segments indefinitely.
cards.explanation: An empty policy list disables segment cleanup.

cards.statement: Kafka forces a disk flush for each record before accepting the next record.
cards.explanation: Kafka writes through the OS pagecache; the OS handles routine flushing.
cards.misconception: Each accepted record requires an immediate disk flush.

cards.statement: With SSL enabled, Kafka's data transfer uses a path other than sendfile.
cards.explanation: Kafka's SSL libraries encrypt in user space, bypassing sendfile.

cards.statement: With cleanup.policy=compact, Kafka keeps at least the latest value for each key in a partition.
cards.explanation: Compaction preserves current key values while removing superseded updates.

cards.statement: On a compacted topic, a keyed record with an empty byte array value deletes that key.
cards.explanation: A deletion tombstone carries a key and a null value.
cards.misconception: An empty value has the deletion meaning of null.

cards.statement: Kafka gives surviving records new offsets after it compacts a partition.
cards.explanation: Records retain their original offsets through compaction.
cards.misconception: Compaction renumbers the surviving records.

cards.statement: After compaction removes a record, Kafka still accepts its offset as a read position.
cards.explanation: Reads at removed offsets resume at the next retained record.

cards.statement: Kafka's log cleaner compacts the active segment while producers append new records.
cards.explanation: The segment receiving writes stays outside compaction.
cards.misconception: The cleaner rewrites the active segment.

cards.statement: Kafka's cleaner recopies log segments while consumers continue reading.
cards.explanation: Background log cleaning leaves reads unblocked.

cards.statement: On a compacted topic, Kafka removes a superseded record before max.compaction.lag.ms has elapsed.
cards.explanation: max.compaction.lag.ms bounds how long a record stays ineligible for compaction, but it is not a hard deadline: cleaning still depends on free log cleaner threads and compaction time.
cards.misconception: max.compaction.lag.ms is a hard deadline by which superseded records are removed.

cards.statement: On a compacted topic, a higher min.cleanable.dirty.ratio makes Kafka clean the log more often.
cards.explanation: A higher dirty-ratio threshold favors fewer, more efficient cleanings.
cards.misconception: A higher threshold increases cleaning frequency.

cards.statement: Kafka enables its log cleaner by default for topics configured with cleanup.policy=compact.
cards.explanation: Kafka starts cleaner threads to maintain compacted topics.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer uses bootstrap.servers as the complete list of brokers it can contact.
cards.explanation: bootstrap.servers provides initial contacts; the producer discovers the remaining brokers.
cards.misconception: Bootstrap servers form a permanent broker allowlist.

cards.statement: A Kafka broker answers metadata requests about other brokers' partitions.
cards.explanation: Any broker supplies cluster-wide partition metadata.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer routes records through the active controller before they reach partition leaders.
cards.explanation: Producers contact partition leaders directly.
cards.misconception: The controller routes producer traffic.

cards.statement: advertised.listeners selects the network interfaces where a broker binds.
cards.explanation: advertised.listeners publishes client addresses; listeners selects bind addresses.
cards.misconception: Advertised addresses determine the broker's bind interfaces.

cards.statement: In a multi-controller KRaft quorum, one controller is active and the others are hot standbys.
cards.explanation: A standby takes over when the active controller fails.

cards.statement: The Kafka docs recommend combined broker and controller mode for critical deployments.
cards.explanation: The docs advise against combined mode in critical deployments.
cards.misconception: Combined mode is recommended for critical deployments.

cards.statement: KRaft needs a majority of controllers alive to keep its metadata quorum available.
cards.explanation: A quorum of 2N + 1 controllers tolerates N controller failures.

cards.statement: A KRaft controller marks a broker offline after missing heartbeats for broker.session.timeout.ms.
cards.explanation: Broker heartbeats keep the broker's controller session active.

cards.statement: Kafka formats blank storage automatically when a new KRaft server starts.
cards.explanation: An operator formats storage with a cluster ID before first startup.
cards.misconception: Server startup automatically initializes blank storage.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, Apache Kafka supports only KRaft for cluster metadata management.
cards.explanation: KRaft controllers manage metadata in Kafka's supported runtime.

cards.statement: After a rolling upgrade, Kafka finalizes the cluster feature level as each broker restarts.
cards.explanation: An administrator finalizes the feature level after verifying the upgraded brokers.
cards.misconception: Binary upgrades automatically finalize metadata features.

cards.statement: A Kafka administrator sets replication factors separately for different topics.
cards.explanation: Topic replication factors determine how many broker copies Kafka maintains.

cards.statement: Kafka replicates a topic by making copies of its individual partition logs.
cards.explanation: Kafka performs replication at the topic-partition level.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer favors the nearest replica for fetching records by default.
cards.explanation: The default replica selector directs reads to the partition leader.
cards.misconception: Consumers choose the closest replica by default.

cards.statement: A follower fetches records from its partition leader to update its own replica log.
cards.explanation: Followers initiate fetches and apply records locally.

cards.statement: A follower's active controller session suffices to retain ISR membership.
cards.explanation: The leader also removes followers that lag beyond replica.lag.time.max.ms.
cards.misconception: Controller connectivity alone ensures ISR membership.

cards.statement: Kafka leaves unclean.leader.election.enable disabled when the setting is omitted.
cards.explanation: The default unclean.leader.election.enable value is false.

cards.statement: The controller gives ISR members priority when selecting a replacement partition leader.
cards.explanation: The controller starts its leader search with the current ISR.

cards.statement: Enabling unclean.leader.election.enable protects committed records when the ISR becomes unavailable.
cards.explanation: An unclean election risks losing committed records missing from the chosen replica.
cards.misconception: An unclean election preserves committed data.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.1, new clusters need an explicit opt-in to enable Eligible Leader Replicas.
cards.explanation: New clusters enable Eligible Leader Replicas by default.
cards.misconception: ELR requires an explicit opt-in on a new cluster.
cards.volatilityNote: The default activation of ELR on new clusters may change.

cards.statement: With broker.rack set, Kafka favors placing a partition's replicas on different racks.
cards.explanation: Rack-aware placement spreads copies across available racks.

cards.statement: With acks=1, a leader failure before replication can lose an acknowledged record.
cards.explanation: The acknowledgement covers the leader's local append.

cards.statement: With acks=all, a write can succeed when the leader is the sole in-sync replica.
cards.explanation: acks=all waits for the current ISR; the default minimum permits one member.

cards.statement: A KafkaProducer with default settings uses acks=1, where the leader responds without waiting for followers.
cards.explanation: KafkaProducer defaults to acks=all: the leader waits for the full set of in-sync replicas to acknowledge a record before the request counts as complete.
cards.misconception: The default acknowledgement mode is acks=1.

cards.statement: With acks=0, RecordMetadata can provide the stored record's broker-assigned offset.
cards.explanation: KafkaProducer returns offset -1 for an acks=0 send.
cards.misconception: acks=0 returns the stored record's offset.

cards.statement: With acks=1, the broker checks min.insync.replicas before accepting a write.
cards.explanation: The write-acceptance minimum applies to acks=all.
cards.misconception: The minimum rejects writes with any acknowledgement mode.

cards.statement: With a raised min.insync.replicas, a leader can report an ISR shortfall after append.
cards.explanation: The broker may detect an ISR drop after appending a record and return a replication error.

cards.statement: With acks=1, consumers can read new records while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas.
cards.explanation: Kafka 4.3 holds consumer visibility until the minimum ISR condition is met.
cards.misconception: acks=1 bypasses the minimum for consumer visibility.
cards.volatilityNote: This strict minimum-ISR visibility rule is recent documentation wording.

cards.statement: Raising min.insync.replicas makes writes more available during replica failures.
cards.explanation: A higher minimum blocks writes sooner as replicas leave the ISR.
cards.misconception: A higher replica minimum increases write availability.

cards.statement: Kafka preserves a committed record while at least one in-sync replica stays alive.
cards.explanation: A surviving in-sync replica protects committed data through failover.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer.send() returns a Future while the producer sends the record asynchronously.
cards.explanation: The Future reports the send result.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer confines record sending to the application thread that constructs the producer.
cards.explanation: KafkaProducer is thread safe; application threads can share it.
cards.misconception: A producer belongs to its constructing thread.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer builds a separate record batch for each partition receiving records.
cards.explanation: Pending records accumulate in per-partition buffers.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer waits for linger.ms to expire before sending a batch that reaches batch.size.
cards.explanation: A full batch becomes ready immediately.
cards.misconception: A full batch still waits for linger.ms.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, KafkaProducer uses a positive linger.ms delay for batching by default.
cards.explanation: The default delay helps the producer build larger batches.

cards.statement: When its send buffer fills, KafkaProducer returns a failed Future immediately.
cards.explanation: send() waits for buffer space, bounded by max.block.ms.
cards.misconception: An exhausted buffer causes immediate failure.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer uses gzip compression for outgoing record batches by default.
cards.explanation: The producer's compression.type defaults to none.
cards.misconception: The producer enables gzip compression by default.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer honors a record's explicit partition even when that record carries a key.
cards.explanation: A valid explicit partition determines a ProducerRecord's destination.

cards.statement: For keyless records with an unspecified partition, KafkaProducer's sticky choice lasts for at least batch.size bytes.
cards.explanation: Sticky placement helps the producer build larger batches.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer's adaptive partitioning favors faster brokers for keyless records by default.
cards.explanation: Adaptive partitioning uses broker performance in placement.

cards.statement: With RoundRobinPartitioner, KafkaProducer can route keyed records by their key hashes.
cards.explanation: RoundRobinPartitioner spreads records regardless of their key hashes.
cards.misconception: RoundRobinPartitioner preserves key-based affinity.

cards.statement: delivery.timeout.ms bounds KafkaProducer's send completion time after send() returns.
cards.explanation: The delivery deadline covers batching, acknowledgements and retries.

cards.statement: The Kafka docs recommend leaving retries unset and controlling retries with delivery.timeout.ms.
cards.explanation: Kafka recommends a delivery deadline over tuning retry counts.

cards.statement: With enable.idempotence=false, retries may reorder partition records with multiple in-flight requests.
cards.explanation: A later batch can succeed before an earlier batch's retry.

cards.statement: With enable.idempotence=false, a retry after a lost acknowledgement retains one log entry.
cards.explanation: An unconfirmed successful write can gain another copy on retry.
cards.misconception: A lost acknowledgement followed by a retry preserves a single copy.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer enables retry deduplication with its default producer settings.
cards.explanation: Compatible default settings enable idempotence.

cards.statement: With enable.idempotence=true and acks=1, KafkaProducer may silently disable idempotence.
cards.explanation: Explicit idempotence makes the acks=1 conflict fail configuration validation.
cards.misconception: Explicit idempotence silently falls back on incompatible acks.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, max.in.flight.requests.per.connection above 5 automatically disables idempotence.
cards.explanation: KafkaProducer rejects the conflict instead of silently falling back.
cards.misconception: An excessive in-flight limit silently switches idempotence off.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer limits its idempotence guarantee to records sent within one producer session.
cards.explanation: A restart establishes a new retry deduplication scope.

cards.statement: Kafka brokers deduplicate retries from an idempotent producer by comparing record keys.
cards.explanation: Brokers identify retries using producer identity and batch sequence numbers.
cards.misconception: Record keys identify duplicate producer retry requests.

cards.statement: A producer with enable.idempotence=true can store duplicate payloads from separate application send() calls.
cards.explanation: Idempotence covers producer retries rather than matching application payloads.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer keeps retrying AuthorizationException until delivery.timeout.ms expires.
cards.explanation: AuthorizationException is non-retriable: KafkaProducer does not resend that record and reports the failure to the send() callback instead.
cards.misconception: Authorization failures are retried until the delivery deadline.

cards.statement: Kafka brokers push newly appended records to KafkaConsumer as they arrive.
cards.explanation: KafkaConsumer retrieves records by requesting them from brokers.
cards.misconception: Brokers initiate delivery when new records arrive.

cards.statement: max.poll.records limits how many records KafkaConsumer fetches in a single broker request.
cards.explanation: max.poll.records caps poll() results; fetched records remain cached.
cards.misconception: The poll limit also limits each broker fetch.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer.wakeup() is safe to call from another thread during a blocked consumer operation.
cards.explanation: wakeup() is the exception to KafkaConsumer's thread-safety restriction.

cards.statement: Kafka assigns a subscribed partition to one consumer within a consumer group.
cards.explanation: Kafka divides consumption using partition ownership.

cards.statement: Consumers with different group.id values share the same consumption position for a partition.
cards.explanation: Each consumer group keeps its own offsets, so every group reads all records of a topic independently, and Kafka supports any number of groups on one topic without duplicating data.
cards.misconception: Different groups share a common reading position.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer.assign() can enlist the group coordinator to distribute its selected partitions.
cards.explanation: Manually assigned consumers act independently.
cards.misconception: Manual assignment uses the group's partition coordination.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer.position() returns its most recently committed offset during active consumption.
cards.explanation: position() identifies the next record; recovery uses committed offsets.
cards.misconception: The current position is the durable restart position.

cards.statement: Kafka stores consumer group offset commits in its __consumer_offsets topic.
cards.explanation: The group coordinator appends offset commits to this internal topic.

cards.statement: With auto.offset.reset=latest, a consumer risks skipping records sent before discovery of a new partition.
cards.explanation: With auto.offset.reset=latest, the consumer starts at a new partition's end, skipping earlier records.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: Kafka preserves an empty group's committed offsets until the topic's record retention expires.
cards.explanation: An empty group's offsets expire according to offsets.retention.minutes.
cards.misconception: Topic data retention determines committed-offset retention.

cards.statement: In a share group, Kafka tracks the acknowledgement of each delivered record separately.
cards.explanation: Share consumers acquire records under a time-limited lock and can acknowledge, release or reject each one; delivery attempts are counted, and a partition may feed several consumers.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer commits offsets periodically under its default configuration.
cards.explanation: enable.auto.commit defaults to true.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: With auto commit, processing the full poll result before the next poll or close gives at-least-once delivery.
cards.explanation: Auto commit can advance past unfinished work at the next poll or close.

cards.statement: With enable.auto.commit=false, processing before commit prevents replay after a crash.
cards.explanation: A crash between processing and commit can cause the work to run again.
cards.misconception: Processing before committing prevents repeated processing.

cards.statement: With enable.auto.commit=false, a consumer can store output and offsets atomically in an external store.
cards.explanation: Atomically saving output with offsets ties a consumer's progress to its stored results.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer sees offset gaps on a transactional topic under either isolation level.
cards.explanation: Transaction markers occupy offsets in the log, and KafkaConsumer filters them out of the records it returns, so the offsets of returned records skip them.

cards.statement: Kafka's default delivery guarantee gives an application exactly one processing attempt per record.
cards.explanation: Kafka defaults to at-least-once delivery.
cards.misconception: Kafka guarantees exactly-once processing by default.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer can invoke a later commitAsync() callback before an earlier call's callback.
cards.explanation: KafkaConsumer invokes commit callbacks in the order of their commit calls.
cards.misconception: Asynchronous commit callbacks can overtake earlier callbacks.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer runs OffsetCommitCallback on a dedicated thread separate from the poll loop.
cards.explanation: KafkaConsumer may execute the callback in a thread calling poll().
cards.misconception: Asynchronous commit callbacks run on a dedicated callback thread.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer.commitSync() can fail if a rebalance transfers partitions before the commit completes.
cards.explanation: The broker may reject a stale owner's commit with CommitFailedException.

cards.statement: A consumer joining a subscribed group can cause Kafka to redistribute its partitions.
cards.explanation: Group membership changes trigger Kafka's rebalance process.

cards.statement: A static member's exceeded max.poll.interval.ms lets Kafka reassign partitions before its session expires.
cards.explanation: Kafka waits for the static member's session timeout before reassignment.
cards.misconception: Static and dynamic members lose their partitions at the same poll deadline.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer selects CooperativeStickyAssignor ahead of RangeAssignor in its default assignor list.
cards.explanation: RangeAssignor precedes CooperativeStickyAssignor in the default preference list.
cards.misconception: The default assignor list already prefers cooperative assignment.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: RangeAssignor distributes partitions independently for subscribed topics.
cards.explanation: RangeAssignor balances each topic's partitions among its subscribers.

cards.statement: With CooperativeStickyAssignor, consumers keep ownership of their unmoved partitions throughout a rebalance.
cards.explanation: With CooperativeStickyAssignor on every group member, rebalances are cooperative: a consumer retains its owned partitions, and only partitions that must move are revoked, then reassigned in a follow-up rebalance.

cards.statement: Consumers sharing group.instance.id can remain active together in one group.
cards.explanation: Kafka fences duplicate static identities.
cards.misconception: Several active consumers can share the same static identity in a group.

cards.statement: ConsumerRebalanceListener exposes a callback for committing offsets before partition reassignment.
cards.explanation: An application can save offsets in onPartitionsRevoked() during a graceful handoff.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer selects group.protocol=consumer when the group.protocol setting is left unset.
cards.explanation: KafkaConsumer defaults to the classic group protocol in Kafka 4.3.
cards.misconception: Server availability of the consumer protocol makes it the client default.
cards.volatilityNote: The documented protocol timeline changes the KafkaConsumer default in a future release.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, group.protocol=consumer uses the client's partition.assignment.strategy for assignment.
cards.explanation: The broker assigns partitions; partition.assignment.strategy is unsupported.
cards.misconception: The consumer protocol retains the classic protocol's client-side assignor setting.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, with group.protocol=consumer, the broker controls the consumer heartbeat interval.
cards.explanation: For group.protocol=consumer, the broker sets group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, KafkaConsumer evaluates SubscriptionPattern locally with group.protocol=consumer.
cards.explanation: The broker evaluates SubscriptionPattern expressions using the RE2J format.
cards.misconception: SubscriptionPattern matching runs in the consumer application.

cards.statement: With transactional.id set, KafkaProducer can atomically commit records across several topics.
cards.explanation: One transaction spans its output partitions and topics.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer.sendOffsetsToTransaction() commits the supplied offsets as soon as the method returns.
cards.explanation: Offsets sent through sendOffsetsToTransaction() commit when their transaction commits.
cards.misconception: Returning from sendOffsetsToTransaction() completes the offset commit.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer begins and commits transactions in a consume-process-produce application.
cards.explanation: KafkaProducer owns the transaction API.
cards.misconception: The consumer manages the transaction for a consume-process-produce loop.

cards.statement: KafkaConsumer returns records from aborted transactions with its default isolation.level setting.
cards.explanation: read_uncommitted includes aborted transactional records.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: With isolation.level=read_committed, KafkaConsumer can read past open transactions to the high watermark.
cards.explanation: read_committed consumers stop at the last stable offset while a transaction remains open.
cards.misconception: A read_committed consumer follows the high watermark through open transactions.

source.title: Kafka 4.3 Consumer and Share Consumer Configs

cards.statement: The Kafka docs recommend enable.auto.commit=true for transactional consume-process-produce applications.
cards.explanation: Use enable.auto.commit=false for transactional offset updates.
cards.misconception: Automatic offset commits fit transactional consume-process-produce processing.

cards.statement: Exactly-once output to an external system depends on that system's cooperation with the application.
cards.explanation: Kafka transactions alone do not coordinate external writes.

cards.statement: With the same transactional.id, initTransactions() aborts a failed producer's transaction left open before commit.
cards.explanation: KafkaProducer resolves a previous transaction for the same transactional.id during initialization. It waits if commit has already started.

cards.statement: Kafka caps a transaction.timeout.ms above transaction.max.timeout.ms at the broker's configured maximum.
cards.explanation: Kafka rejects a requested transaction timeout above the broker maximum.
cards.misconception: Kafka silently clamps an excessive transaction timeout.

cards.statement: Since Kafka 4.0, Kafka advances a transactional producer's epoch for successive transactions.
cards.explanation: New epochs keep late writes out of subsequent transactions.

cards.statement: KafkaProducer.abortTransaction() also rewinds KafkaConsumer to the aborted transaction's input records.
cards.explanation: After an abort, the application must reset the consumer position explicitly so that it reprocesses the records handled by the aborted transaction.
cards.misconception: Aborting a producer transaction also restores the consumer's current position.

cards.statement: Kafka Streams represents the changing result of a grouped KStream aggregation as another KStream.
cards.explanation: An aggregation yields a KTable whose updates describe the evolving result.
cards.misconception: Aggregating a grouped KStream produces another KStream.

cards.statement: Kafka Streams applications use Interactive Queries to inspect local state stores through read-only views.
cards.explanation: Interactive Queries exposes read operations, protecting Kafka Streams state from external changes.

cards.statement: For a fixed topology, Kafka Streams derives its stream-task count from input partitions.
cards.explanation: Adding Kafka Streams instances redistributes existing stream tasks instead of creating extra tasks.

cards.statement: A Kafka Streams windowed aggregation accepts late records after the window's grace period expires.
cards.explanation: Kafka Streams discards records for a window after stream time passes its end plus the grace period.
cards.misconception: A window continues accepting late updates beyond its grace period.

cards.statement: Kafka Streams runs with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 unless an application overrides it.
cards.explanation: Kafka Streams defaults processing.guarantee to at_least_once; an application gets exactly-once processing only by setting exactly_once_v2 explicitly.
cards.misconception: Kafka Streams enables exactly_once_v2 processing by default.

cards.statement: Kafka Connect runs a source connector's tasks to deliver topic records to an external database.
cards.explanation: A source connector imports external records into Kafka topics.
cards.misconception: Source connector tasks export Kafka records to external systems.

cards.statement: Distributed Kafka Connect workers persist configurations, offsets and statuses in Kafka topics.
cards.explanation: Compacted internal Kafka topics preserve distributed Kafka Connect workers' shared state.

cards.statement: Kafka Connect chooses key and value serialization formats from the connector class.
cards.explanation: key.converter and value.converter select formats independently of the connector.
cards.misconception: The connector class determines Kafka's key and value serialization formats.

cards.statement: A configured Kafka Connect transformation can redirect a source record to a different topic.
cards.explanation: Kafka Connect routing transformations change a record's topic before publication.

cards.statement: In distributed mode, Kafka Connect's worker settings alone determine exactly-once source delivery.
cards.explanation: Kafka Connect's exactly-once source delivery depends on the source connector supporting it.
cards.misconception: Enabling exactly-once in the workers suffices regardless of the source connector's capabilities.

cards.statement: Kafka accepts custom listener names when listener.security.protocol.map supplies their security protocols.
cards.explanation: Kafka listener names describe their purpose; the mapping independently specifies the protocol.

cards.statement: With an SSL listener, a Kafka broker requests client certificates when ssl.client.auth is left unset.
cards.explanation: ssl.client.auth defaults to none; client certificate authentication is optional to configure.
cards.misconception: An SSL listener enables client certificate authentication automatically.

cards.statement: With security.protocol=SSL, KafkaProducer leaves broker hostname verification disabled by default.
cards.explanation: With SSL, KafkaProducer checks broker hostnames using the default https identification algorithm.
cards.misconception: Kafka's TLS hostname verification requires an explicit opt-in.

cards.statement: For SASL_SSL connections, KafkaProducer's default sasl.mechanism is PLAIN.
cards.explanation: sasl.mechanism defaults to GSSAPI (Kerberos) for SASL connections, so a client that uses PLAIN has to set sasl.mechanism=PLAIN explicitly.
cards.misconception: SASL_SSL selects PLAIN as the client's default authentication mechanism.

cards.statement: The Kafka docs recommend TLS transport when Kafka clients use SASL/PLAIN in production.
cards.explanation: TLS protects the passwords transmitted by SASL/PLAIN.

cards.statement: By default, Kafka stores SCRAM authentication credentials in the cluster's KRaft metadata log.
cards.explanation: KRaft metadata contains SCRAM identities, including salts and derived keys.

cards.statement: StandardAuthorizer grants ordinary users access when a resource's matching ACL set is empty.
cards.explanation: StandardAuthorizer reserves resources with an empty matching ACL set for super users by default.
cards.misconception: The authorizer permits ordinary users when a resource has no matching ACL.

cards.statement: StandardAuthorizer can apply the literal topic pattern orders* to topics named orders-new.
cards.explanation: Literal patterns match exact names; Kafka reserves the standalone * for a wildcard.
cards.misconception: Literal topic resource patterns expand a trailing asterisk into prefix matches.

cards.statement: StandardAuthorizer gives a matching deny ACL precedence over allow ACLs for an ordinary user.
cards.explanation: For ordinary users, StandardAuthorizer honors a matching deny even when a broader ACL allows the operation.

cards.statement: For a specific ACL host entry, Kafka matches the client by its IP address.
cards.explanation: Specific ACL host entries identify permitted or denied client IP addresses.
cards.volatilityNote: ACL host-matching formats are evolving in planned releases.
